A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe the same GPT-2/DPO toxicity study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original neuron-ablation, activation-patching and toxicity-projection results, including Tables 1–2 and the neuron-group analyses.

after.justification: V2 reports retained and revised intervention experiments in Table 1, neuron-projection analyses, and vocabulary-projection results in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The per-neuron projection calculation, four neuron groups and mean post-DPO activation-patching procedure remain unchanged. The restriction to 128 toxic neurons changes the diagnostic intervention settings rather than the underlying group-patching method.

E1.justification: Both retain RealToxicityPrompts challenge prompts, Jigsaw probe data, Wikitext-2 and Wikipedia token-matching evaluation. The new vocabulary-projection analysis examines existing model neurons without adding a dataset, domain or evaluated task.

E2.justification: GPT-2 and DPO remain the reference models. V1 Table 1 additionally compares DPO with its top seven toxic-neuron key vectors scaled by factors of 2, 5 and 10; these comparison variants disappear from v2. Newly cited intervention methods are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: The central intervention design changes from ablation sweeps covering 100–1,000 toxic neurons and up to 2,000 positively activated toxic neurons to a fixed 128-neuron set, including a 36-neuron positive-activation subset. Figure 1a also replaces 200-neuron ablation with 128-neuron ablation. Model, datasets, metrics and 20-token averaging remain fixed. Probe provenance changes from reuse to described training, without establishing actual retraining.

E4.justification: V2 removes the neuron-count sensitivity sweep, key-vector-scaling tests and standalone AP+ patching test. It adds Appendix B's ranked value-vector/token analysis to distinguish directly toxic neurons from broadly aligned neurons. The negative-activation, cumulative-neuron and layerwise group analyses remain after relocation; they are not new analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and aggregate projections without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. Averaging over prompts and generated tokens is unchanged.

E6.justification: The headline attribution changes from 31.8% for v1's broad TP− group to 4.9% under v2's narrower toxic-neuron definition. V2 Table 1 reports toxicity of 0.404 for patching 128 toxic neurons and 0.409 for ablating them; these use different settings from v1's sweep. Earlier sweep, scaling and AP+-only entries disappear. Shared group-patching results remain identical, including 0.114 for all groups versus 0.208 for DPO. Appendix B adds decoded-token findings.

T1.justification: Equation 1 retains the same projection difference, and Appendix A retains the MLP expansion in Equations 2–3. The four-group construction and proportional-projection assumption remain. Changed notation and explanatory prose introduce no new mathematical result or proof.

C1.justification: The central claim of distributed toxicity reduction across four neuron groups remains. V2 narrows the quantified toxic-neuron attribution from 31.8% to 4.9% and presents the existing group-patching experiment as an explicit intervention contribution that replicates DPO's toxicity reduction.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving layer-to-layer propagation, indirect effects of neurons without toxic token projections, and exclusion of toxicity-increasing neurons explaining patching's advantage. It removes cautions about unrealistic scaling and averaged patching, while retaining the single-probe and feature-composition limitations. It also changes the claim that the top three groups individually reduce toxicity to a claim about each group.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the 128-neuron target and 36-neuron positive subset, and supplies vector identities and ranks in Appendix B. It describes training the probe where v1 described using Lee et al.'s vector, without additional training details resolving whether retraining occurred. The code link and mean-patching implementation remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Elhage, Ferrando, nostalgebraist, Shazeer and Suau references, while removing Lange, Lieberum and Tan. It connects its critique to superposition and its intervention findings to Whispering Experts. Lee et al. remains the central comparison and research-positioning reference.

P1.justification: The title and much of the abstract, introduction, setup, analysis, discussion and conclusion are rewritten. The standalone activation-patching section is integrated into Section 4.3, limitations become a separate section, and the appendices are reorganized. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the experimental changes.

P2.justification: V1 Tables 1–2 are consolidated into v2 Table 1, and a vocabulary table is added in Appendix B. V1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 1b, while the old Figure 1b moves to Appendix D. Figure 2 replaces its 500-neuron projection panel with the previously appended 3,000–3,200-neuron activation panel. Resizing, relabeling and relocation substantially revise the visual organization.

improvement.justification: V2 improves organization and adds useful token-level evidence, but drops the AP+-only result (v1 Table 2: toxicity 0.455 versus 0.453 untreated) while asserting that patching each group reduces toxicity. It also removes the qualification that prompt-specific patching would better approximate DPO than averaged patching. These changes modestly weaken evidential completeness and qualification of claims, despite retaining the core findings.
